reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The commonest compressive mononeuropathy of the lower limb, typically injured where the nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck, presenting with foot drop and a high-stepping gait
Weak ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension (deep peroneal) and weak foot eversion (superficial peroneal) are found, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral lower leg
Ankle inversion (tibialis posterior) and plantarflexion are preserved, which distinguishes a peroneal lesion from an L5 radiculopathy or a sciatic or lumbosacral plexus lesion

Common precipitants include habitual leg crossing, prolonged squatting or kneeling, rapid weight loss ('slimmer's palsy'), tight plaster casts or boots, and malpositioning during anaesthesia or bed rest
A tibialis anterior that is weaker than tibialis posterior, with a positive Tinel sign at the fibular neck, favours a peroneal lesion over an L5 root lesion
Structural causes such as an intraneural or extraneural ganglion, a Baker cyst, nerve sheath tumour or trauma should be excluded, particularly when onset is painful or progressive

Management centres on removing external compression, an ankle-foot orthosis to correct foot drop and prevent contracture, physiotherapy, and surgical decompression or excision when a structural lesion is identified
reference.pathophysiology: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve is the lateral division of the sciatic nerve, carrying predominantly L4-S1 fibres. After separating in the popliteal fossa it curves around the lateral aspect of the fibular neck, where it lies superficially against bone with little protective soft tissue before dividing into the deep peroneal nerve (ankle and toe dorsiflexors, first dorsal web-space sensation) and the superficial peroneal nerve (evertors, dorsal foot sensation). This superficial, tethered course over rigid bone makes it highly vulnerable to external compression, stretch during knee flexion and inversion injury, and to focal masses such as ganglia. Injury produces focal demyelination with conduction block in mild cases and axonal loss in severe or prolonged compression, manifesting as weakness of dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion with corresponding sensory loss.
additionalDifferentials: Motor neurone disease presenting with foot drop
Anterior compartment syndrome or tibialis anterior tendon rupture
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies seeking conduction block or slowing across the fibular head
Needle electromyography comparing peroneal-innervated with tibial-innervated and other L5 muscles to exclude a root lesion
High-resolution ultrasound of the nerve at the fibular neck to detect a ganglion or focal enlargement
MRI of the knee and proximal leg when a structural or intraneural cystic lesion is suspected
Lumbar spine imaging if L5 radiculopathy remains a competing diagnosis
Screening for diabetes or systemic neuropathy in atypical or bilateral cases
redFlags: Painful or rapidly progressive foot drop suggesting a mass, intraneural ganglion or inflammatory neuropathy
Weakness extending beyond the peroneal distribution (for example weak inversion or plantarflexion) indicating a sciatic, plexus or root lesion
Bilateral foot drop raising concern for polyneuropathy or motor neurone disease
Calf swelling, tense compartment or severe disproportionate pain suggesting compartment syndrome
reference.prognosis: Neuropraxic palsies from transient compression usually recover over weeks to a few months once the precipitant is removed, and an ankle-foot orthosis maintains function in the interim. Lesions with substantial axonal loss or an unresected structural cause recover more slowly and less completely, and may leave a persistent foot drop.
pitfalls: Confusing a peroneal palsy with L5 radiculopathy by failing to test ankle inversion and plantarflexion
Missing an intraneural ganglion or nerve sheath tumour in painful or recurrent presentations
Attributing foot drop solely to positioning while overlooking a persisting structural cause
Not fitting an ankle-foot orthosis early, allowing an equinus contracture to develop
Overlooking a proximal sciatic lesion in which the peroneal division is selectively vulnerable
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
